title: Quality Control, Westgard Rules, and Regulatory Frameworks

cards.front: What does the 1-2s Westgard rule mean and what action does it require?
cards.back: One control result beyond 2 SD: a WARNING rule - evaluate the remaining rules before accepting the run. It does not reject the run by itself.

cards.front: State the classic Westgard rejection rules.
cards.back: 1-3s (one control beyond 3 SD), 2-2s (two controls beyond 2 SD on the same side, within-run or between-run), R-4s (range between two controls exceeds 4 SD in one run).

cards.front: 1-2s = [[1]] rule. 1-3s and R-4s target [[2]] error. 2-2s, 4-1s, and 8x target [[3]] error.
cards.back: 1: warning  2: random  3: systematic

cards.front: What is the R-4s rule and what error does it detect?
cards.back: Range between two control results in one run exceeds 4 SD (one high, one low) - detects large random error.

cards.front: What is a Levey-Jennings chart?
cards.back: Control results plotted over run order or date, centered on the established mean with lines at plus/minus 1, 2, and 3 SD.

cards.front: SDI = (observed value minus [[1]]) divided by [[2]]. CV = SD divided by [[3]], times 100.
cards.back: 1: peer mean  2: peer standard deviation  3: mean

cards.front: What are the CLIA complexity categories?
cards.back: Waived, moderate complexity, and high complexity; obligations (QC, PT, personnel) scale with complexity. Waived still requires following manufacturer instructions.

cards.front: What must be done after an unsatisfactory proficiency testing result?
cards.back: Root-cause investigation, documented corrective action, and assessment of impact on patient results - not just a repeat challenge.

cards.front: LOD = limit of [[1]]; LOQ = limit of [[2]], defined by acceptable [[3]] and accuracy.
cards.back: 1: detection  2: quantitation  3: precision

cards.front: How are precision and accuracy distinguished?
cards.back: Precision = agreement of repeated measurements (SD, CV). Accuracy (trueness) = closeness to the true value (recovery, method comparison). They are independent.

cards.front: Which validation study addresses analytical specificity?
cards.back: Interference testing (hemolysis, icterus, lipemia, drugs, cross-reactivity).

cards.front: Reference intervals must be established or [[1]] for the local population and method, reported with [[2]] and the caveat that intervals vary by laboratory, method, age, sex, and [[3]].
cards.back: 1: verified  2: units  3: population

cards.front: What biosafety level applies to most clinical laboratory work, and what does M. tuberculosis culture require?
cards.back: BSL-2 for most clinical work (BSC for aerosols, bloodborne pathogen standard); M. tuberculosis culture manipulation requires BSL-3 with respiratory protection and controlled access.

cards.front: What is the hierarchy of controls in laboratory safety?
cards.back: Engineering controls (safety cabinets, sealed centrifuge cups) outrank work practice controls, which outrank personal protective equipment.

cards.front: The 8x rule rejects when [[1]] consecutive control results fall on [[2]] of the mean, detecting a systematic [[3]].
cards.back: 1: eight  2: one side  3: shift or trend

cards.front: What must QC event documentation include?
cards.back: Control values, the Westgard rule triggered, suspected cause, corrective action, and disposition of patient results - traceable and never overwritten.

cards.front: What is the difference between method verification and full validation?
cards.back: Verification confirms a manufacturer-established method performs as claimed locally; full validation characterizes a new/modified method (precision, accuracy, LOD/LOQ, linearity, interferences, reference intervals).

cards.front: Quality control rules detect [[1]] within a stable process; proficiency testing detects [[2]] problems; both must be [[3]] when unsatisfactory.
cards.back: 1: error  2: accuracy  3: investigated and documented

title: Preanalytic Errors, Order of Draw, POCT, and Lab Math

cards.front: State the standard order of draw for venipuncture tubes.
cards.back: Blood culture bottles, light blue (citrate), serum (red/tiger), green (heparin), lavender (EDTA), gray (fluoride/oxalate).

cards.front: Why does the order of draw matter?
cards.back: Additive carryover: EDTA into citrate falsely prolongs PT/aPTT; citrate into potassium samples falsely lowers potassium.

cards.front: Mnemonic for order of draw: Boys Can Really Have Easy Girls = [[1]] cultures, [[2]], Red, Heparin, EDTA, Gray.
cards.back: 1: Blood  2: Citrate (light blue)

cards.front: What happens if a light blue citrate coagulation tube is underfilled?
cards.back: Excess citrate relative to blood falsely prolongs PT and aPTT; fill within the manufacturer's range (commonly 90-110 percent) or reject per procedure.

cards.front: Which chemistry results are typically affected by hemolysis?
cards.back: Potassium, LDH, AST, magnesium, phosphate rise (falsely elevated); some colorimetric methods are biased - comment or reject per validated HIL limits.

cards.front: A mislabeled specimen must be [[1]] and [[2]]; relabeling is [[3]].
cards.back: 1: rejected  2: recollected  3: never permitted

cards.front: Name three objective specimen rejection criteria.
cards.back: Wrong/mismatched identifiers, clotted EDTA or citrate specimens, insufficient volume (especially citrate underfill), hemolysis beyond validated limits, transport outside validated temperature/time windows.

cards.front: What quality elements are required for point-of-care testing?
cards.back: Operator training and documented competency, QC with lockout where available, consumable lot tracking, maintenance logs, and result documentation in the medical record.

cards.front: CLIA-waived status does not waive [[1]] instructions or laboratory [[2]]; every operator still needs documented [[3]].
cards.back: 1: manufacturer  2: oversight  3: competency

cards.front: Which factors bias point-of-care glucose meters?
cards.back: Hematocrit extremes, perfusion, oxygen tension, and interfering substances (for example, maltose, uric acid, acetaminophen on some chemistries); capillary and venous values can differ.

cards.front: C1V1 = [[1]]: to make 50 mL of 2 mol/L from 10 mol/L stock, use [[2]] mL of stock plus 40 mL of diluent.
What is the difference between a 1:10 dilution and 1 part sample plus 10 parts diluent?
cards.back: A 1:10 dilution is 1 part sample in 10 total (9 parts diluent); 1 part plus 10 parts gives 1:11 total. Dilution factor = total volume / sample volume.

cards.front: Glucose: mmol/L = mg/dL x [[1]] (or divided by [[2]]). Creatinine: micromol/L = mg/dL x [[3]].
What does 0.9 percent NaCl mean in laboratory units?
cards.back: 0.9 grams of NaCl per 100 mL of solution (9 g/L, about 154 mmol/L sodium, approximately isotonic).

cards.front: How is a urine culture concentration calculated from a dilution plate?
cards.back: CFU/mL = colonies / plated volume x dilution factor. Example: 45 colonies on 0.01 mL of a 1:100 dilution = 45 / 0.01 x 100 = 450,000 CFU/mL.

cards.front: Each 10-fold dilution step should drop colony counts roughly [[1]]-fold; this serves as a [[2]] check before reporting.
cards.back: 1: ten  2: consistency

cards.front: Which preanalytic changes falsely raise serum potassium?
cards.back: Hemolysis (traumatic draw), fist clenching with prolonged tourniquet, delayed separation of serum from cells; infusion contamination/dilution can falsely lower it.

cards.front: What is the prozone (hook) effect and how is it resolved?
cards.back: Extremely high analyte/antibody concentrations give false-negative agglutination or sandwich immunoassay results; dilution of the specimen restores the true positive.
